args.title: dpa-counter-markup-analysis-memo.docx
args.body:
PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
DRAFT — NEGOTIATION ANALYSIS MEMORANDUM

TO: Engagement Partner and DPA Negotiation Team
FROM: White-Collar Defense & Investigations Group
RE: Government Counter-Markup Analysis — Deferred Prosecution Agreement for Financial Services Company
DATE: [Current Date]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This memorandum provides a comprehensive negotiation analysis of the government's counter-markup to the Deferred Prosecution Agreement ("DPA") for the financial services company client. It compares the government's counter-markup against (i) the original DPA and (ii) our initial markup, and identifies, for each deviation introduced by the government, the negotiation position, the risk profile, and recommended response. The analysis reconciles the counter-markup against the disclosure schedules (Schedule 3.7 and Schedule 5.2) and the survival matrix (Exhibit B), and incorporates the controlling client instruction from deal team correspondence regarding the priority ordering of concessions.

Control Instruction. The most recent partner instruction (which supersedes all earlier messages to the contrary) directs that the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. All analysis below reflects this controlling priority ordering.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
II. DOCUMENTS REVIEWED
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

• Original DPA (Deal Materials, Matter File 26) — operative agreement containing representations and warranties, covenants, conditions, closing, indemnification, and termination provisions.
• Government Counter-Markup (Counterparty Markup, Matter File 52) — the government's revision introducing deviations to the indemnification cap, the basket type, the Material Adverse Effect definition, and the survival period.
• Schedules and Exhibits (Matter File 104) — Schedule 3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries), Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), and Exhibit B (survival matrix).
• Deal Team Correspondence (Matter File 130) — partner email chain; the latest message controls the negotiation priorities.
• Our Initial Markup — the firm's starting position reflected in the base DPA materials (the position from which the government's counter-markup departs).

The scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
III. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF DEVIATIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The government's counter-markup accepts most firm-standard (and our initial markup's) provisions, but introduces four material deviations that must be addressed:

1. Indemnification Cap — silently reduced from the level in our initial markup.
2. Basket Conversion — converted from a deductible basket to a tipping basket.
3. Material Adverse Effect (MAE) Definition — adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter.
4. Survival Period — a new limitation period shortens survival for the core representations, contradicting Exhibit B's survival matrix.

Of these, Deviation 2 (basket conversion) is conceded per the controlling client instruction, and Deviation 4 (survival period reduction) is a designated walk-away issue. Deviations 1 (indemnification cap) and 3 (MAE carve-outs) require careful positioning in light of the schedules.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- A. Deviation 1 — Indemnification Cap Reduction -------------------------

WHAT THE GOVERNMENT'S MARKUP DOES. The counterparty's revision silently reduces the indemnification cap from the level reflected in our initial markup. No rationale is stated in the markup; the reduction appears as a numeric change to the cap provision.

IMPACT. A reduced indemnification cap directly reduces the maximum exposure the financial services company can recover (or against which it is protected) in the event of a breach of the DPA's representations and warranties or covenants. Critically, Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. Read together, a reduced cap combined with the retained-liabilities schedule means that certain liabilities that had been expected to fall beneath the protection of the indemnity could now exceed the available cap, effectively pushing those liabilities back onto the client.

RISK ASSESSMENT. Medium-High. The cap reduction is a direct economic give-back against our initial position. Absent a countervailing concession, accepting the reduced cap while retaining the full scope of represented liabilities under Schedule 5.2 would leave the client under-protected against precisely the retained liabilities the schedules disclose. The government has not offered any corresponding adjustment (e.g., a higher basket, a narrower set of indemnified losses, or a shorter indemnity period) that would justify a lower cap.

RECOMMENDED POSITION. Resist the silent cap reduction. Given that the client is conceding the basket conversion (see Deviation 2 below), the case for maintaining the indemnification cap from our initial markup is strengthened — the concession on basket mechanics should be leveraged to hold the line on cap quantum. We should counter with the original cap figure and, at most, consider a modest step-down tied to a corresponding narrowing of Schedule 5.2 indemnified items, clearly flagged rather than silent. Any movement on the cap must be explicitly conditioned on clarification of which Schedule 5.2 liabilities remain indemnified.

--- B. Deviation 2 — Basket Conversion (Deductible → Tipping) ----------------

WHAT THE GOVERNMENT'S MARKUP DOES. The counter-markup converts the indemnification basket from a deductible basket to a tipping basket.

EXPLANATION OF THE DIFFERENCE. Under a deductible basket, losses must exceed the basket threshold before any recovery is available, and once the threshold is crossed the indemnitor pays only the excess above the threshold. Under a tipping basket, once aggregate losses cross the threshold, the indemnitor is liable for the entire amount from the first dollar (i.e., the threshold is "tipped" and full liability attaches). The tipping basket is more favorable to the indemnitee (the client), because it lowers the effective recovery point once the threshold is crossed.

IMPACT ON CLIENT. For the financial services company as the party seeking the benefit of indemnification protections, a tipping basket is more favorable than a deductible. The conversion is therefore a government concession to the client's benefit.

RECOMMENDED POSITION. CONCEDE. Per the controlling partner instruction, the client will concede the basket conversion. Because the conversion inures to the client's benefit (tipping baskets are more favorable than deductibles), this is a low-cost concession that provides negotiating capital to deploy against the more consequential deviations (especially the cap reduction and the survival period). We should accept the tipping basket in exchange for, or at least in parallel with, holding our position on the indemnification cap. This is a controlled, intentional concession — not a capitulation.

--- C. Deviation 3 — MAE Definition Adds Regulatory Action Carve-Outs -------

WHAT THE GOVERNMENT'S MARKUP DOES. The counter-markup adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter."

IMPACT. MAE carve-outs operate to except certain events from the definition of a Material Adverse Effect — meaning that such events would not constitute (or could be deemed not to constitute) an MAE, thereby limiting the client's ability to invoke an MAE condition or remedy. Adding carve-outs for regulatory action of the exact kind at issue in this matter is highly consequential because the DPA's subject matter is regulatory/SEC/enforcement exposure for a financial services company.

CRITICAL INTERPLAY WITH SCHEDULE 3.7. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. Those two inquiries intersect directly with the MAE carve-outs the markup seeks to add. If the carve-outs are accepted as drafted, the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7 would fall squarely within the carve-outs and would be excluded from constituting (or contributing to) a Material Adverse Effect. This would materially erode the client's ability to rely on those pending inquiries as the basis for an MAE determination, even though they are the exact exposures the client has disclosed and the core of the regulatory risk in this engagement.

RISK ASSESSMENT. High. Unlike the basket conversion (which benefits the client), these regulatory carve-outs target the heart of the client's disclosed regulatory exposure. The interplay with Schedule 3.7 means the carve-outs are not hypothetical — they would directly neutralize the pending-inquiry risk disclosures. Accepting the carve-outs as drafted would gut the protective value of the MAE definition as it relates to the precise regulatory matters at the center of the DPA.

RECOMMENDED POSITION. Reject the carve-outs as drafted. At minimum, the carve-outs must be narrowed so that they do not sweep in the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7. If the government insists on retaining regulatory-action carve-outs, we should counter with carve-outs that expressly carve in (i.e., do not except) the Schedule 3.7 pending inquiries, or that limit the exception to regulatory actions not disclosed on the schedules. This reconciliation of the markup with the schedules is mandatory per the Schedules and Exhibits materials. We should not accept broad regulatory-action carve-outs without explicit preservation of the Schedule 3.7 disclosures as potentially MAE-constituting events.

--- D. Deviation 4 — Survival Period Reduction ------------------------------

WHAT THE GOVERNMENT'S MARKUP DOES. The counter-markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations.

IMPACT ON EXHIBIT B. The Schedules and Exhibits materials state that Exhibit B sets the survival matrix, and that the markup's limitation-period change directly contradicts Exhibit B. A shortened survival period would cut off the client's right to pursue claims for breaches of the core representations after a shorter window than our initial markup and the survival matrix contemplate. For a financial services company facing regulatory exposure, the core representations concerning compliance, financial condition, and regulatory matters are precisely where breaches may come to light only after an extended period of time. Compressing the survival window for those representations would be materially adverse to the client.

RISK ASSESSMENT. WALK-AWAY ISSUE — Critical. Per the controlling client instruction, any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue. This is the highest-priority deviation and must not be conceded under any circumstances. The government's change contradicts the survival matrix at Exhibit B, and the schedules control over general statements.

RECOMMENDED POSITION. Hold firm at our initial markup's survival period as reflected in the Exhibit B survival matrix. Do not accept any reduction. Treat the survival-period reduction as a non-negotiable, transaction-blocking point. This is the central issue on which the client's position is fixed, and we should communicate early and unambiguously that we will not trade on this provision. If the government presses, we should signal that no agreement is reachable on the government's survival terms, invoking the walk-away posture rather than continuing to negotiate the point.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
V. RECONCILIATION WITH DISCLOSURE SCHEDULES AND EXHIBITS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Schedules and Exhibits materials require the deliverable to reconcile BOTH the scheduled exceptions and the counterparty markup against the base materials. Key reconciliation findings:

Schedule 3.7 (Pending Regulatory Inquiries): Two pending regulatory inquiries are disclosed. These intersect directly with the markup's MAE carve-outs (Deviation 3). Any carve-out for regulatory action must be drafted to preserve the Schedule 3.7 inquiries as potentially MAE-constituting events. The scheduled exceptions control over the general statements; accordingly, the carve-outs cannot be read to override the Schedule 3.7 disclosures.

Schedule 5.2 (Retained Liabilities): Retained liabilities listed on Schedule 5.2 are the liabilities the markup's indemnification changes (Deviation 1 — cap reduction) would silently shift. The cap reduction must not be permitted to erode coverage for the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities. Any cap movement must be expressly reconciled against Schedule 5.2.

Exhibit B (Survival Matrix): Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change (Deviation 4) contradicts. Because this is a walk-away issue, we hold Exhibit B's survival terms without modification.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. INTEGRATED NEGOTIATION STRATEGY AND RECOMMENDED LEVERAGE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Given the controlling partner instruction on priority ordering, the recommended negotiation posture is as follows:

1. Conceed the basket conversion (Deviation 2). This is the controlled concession that buys negotiating capital. It also inures to the client's benefit (tipping basket), so the cost is minimal.

2. Use the basket concession to hold the indemnification cap (Deviation 1). Counter the reduced cap with our initial cap figure. Frame acceptance of the basket conversion as consideration for maintaining the cap and reconciling Schedule 5.2 retained-liability coverage.

3. Reject the MAE regulatory carve-outs as drafted (Deviation 3), and replace them with carve-outs that preserve the Schedule 3.7 pending inquiries as potentially MAE-constituting events.

4. Do not move on the survival period (Deviation 4). This is the walk-away issue. Communicate that no agreement is reachable on a reduced survival period, and hold the Exhibit B survival matrix.

Proposed Tabling Order for Negotiation Sessions:
• Open with the concession on the basket conversion to establish a constructive tone.
• Then present the walk-away position on the survival period as a threshold matter, so that the government understands the immovable boundary early.
• Negotiate the indemnification cap and MAE carve-outs within the bounds set by Devations 1 and 3, leveraging the basket concession and the acknowledged walk-away on survival.

Key Risk to Flag: The government's deviations are interconnected. Accepting the basket conversion while conceding the cap reduction, the MAE carve-outs, and the survival-period cut would collectively strip the client of meaningful indemnification protection. The basket concession must be carefully deployed so that it is not read as a signal of broader willingness to give ground on the other, more severe deviations.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. CONCLUSION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The government's counter-markup introduces four material deviations. The client's controlling instruction concedes the basket conversion (Deviation 2), which is in the client's favor and provides negotiating capital. The survival-period reduction (Deviation 4) is a designated walk-away issue and must remain non-negotiable. The indemnification cap reduction (Deviation 1) and the MAE regulatory carve-outs (Deviation 3) must be resisted and carefully reconciled with Schedule 5.2 and Schedule 3.7 respectively, using the basket concession as leverage. The deliverable reflects these priorities and provides a clear negotiation roadmap.

Respectfully submitted,
White-Collar Defense & Investigations Group

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[END OF MEMORANDUM]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
